Sunday, Delhi hostel

Kunal played an Assamese song on his speaker today, by accident, just scrolling. I had to leave the room. I sat on the stairs and cried a little, which is stupid, because I'm nineteen. It was the Bihu song the neighbours play every April in Jorhat. I could smell the pitha and see the lane with the big jackfruit tree. Here nobody says 'kene asa'. I speak Hindi and English all day and my own language is only in my head. The strange thing is, when I was home I complained about everything: the power cuts, the gossip, the mud. In my head now, the lane is always sunny and everyone is smiling. I know it wasn't like that. I miss it anyway. I miss a Jorhat that maybe never existed.

Chandrika

Sunday night, Chennai

Pongal was quiet this year. No Paati, no cousins, no village. So I made sakkarai pongal in my tiny flat, and it boiled over just like it should, and I shouted 'Pongalo pongal!' alone in my kitchen. Then I video-called Amma, who cried a little when she saw the pot. After that, I did something new. I invited Parul from work and two neighbours I barely knew. Parul had never had pongal. She took three helpings. We sat on the floor and talked till ten. I realised home isn't only back in Madurai. It can be the smell of jaggery, the call with Amma, and people on my floor learning my festival. I still ache for the village. But the ache feels warm now, not heavy.

Madhuri

passage: Last month, Ishita, my closest friend, went through a breakup, and she called me every night crying. I'm Nazia, and at first I cried with her, every call. After a week, I was exhausted and snapping at everyone at work. Then I noticed something: I was carrying her sadness like it was mine. So I tried a little sentence in my head: 'This is her feeling, not mine. I can be with it without becoming it.' I still listened every night. But I also took breaks, went for a walk before bed, and stopped reading sad posts about breakups. And I did one practical thing: on Saturday I took her out for dosa and a long walk by the lake. She laughed for the first time in weeks. I felt lighter too, not because I cared less, but because I cared better.
